descriptive ethical relativism|descripti: The empirical claim that *different societies have different moral codes* (Rachels's claim 1); *True. It's empirically verifiable* (slide 17). See [Cultures differ in their moral codes, but relativism does not follow](#/libs7102-l3/rachels-six-claims-and-the-argument).
normative ethical relativism|cultural re: Rachels's claims 2–6: no objective standard to judge one societal code better than another, no universal truth in ethics, *the moral code of a society determines what is right in that society*; *A mistake with serious consequences* (slide 17). See [Cultures differ in their moral codes, but relativism does not follow](#/libs7102-l3/rachels-six-claims-and-the-argument).
cultural differences argument: Rachels's name for the argument from *different societies have different moral codes* to *there is no objective truth in morality*; *not valid*, because of *a move from "is" to "ought"* (slide 18). See [Cultures differ in their moral codes, but relativism does not follow](#/libs7102-l3/rachels-six-claims-and-the-argument).
appeal to hypocrisy: *"You are hypocritical, therefore your claim can be ignored"*: a fallacy, because whether an action is wrong and whether the speaker acts on their own judgement are *two entirely distinct and independent issues* (slide 12). See ["Do not judge" defeats itself, and hypocrisy does not make a judgment wrong](#/libs7102-l3/why-we-should-judge).
hypermoralism: *Demanding purity and perfect alignment, no tolerance*; with relativism (*too much tolerance*), one of two *serious problems* that *both can connect to polarization* (slide 6). See [The relativist says no culture's morality is better than another's](#/libs7102-l3/what-the-relativist-says).
moral objectivism|objectivist: Pojman: *There is a fact of the matter as to whether any given action is morally permissible or impermissible: a fact of the matter that does not depend solely on social custom or individual acceptance* (slide 28). Not Ayn Rand's Objectivism and not being objective (slide 24). See [Objectivism asks whether there is a moral fact; absolutism whether a rule is never broken](#/libs7102-l3/objectivism-absolutism-and-being-objective).
moral absolutism|absolutist: Pojman: *There is at least one principle that ought never to be violated* (slide 28). Objectivists can be absolutist (Kant) or non-absolutist (utilitarians, virtue ethics), and a relativist can be absolutist (slide 29). See [Objectivism asks whether there is a moral fact; absolutism whether a rule is never broken](#/libs7102-l3/objectivism-absolutism-and-being-objective).
being objective: A description of someone's *psychology – they are impartial, unbiased (e.g. like a good judge, referee)*; it *says nothing about their position on the universality of moral values* (slide 24). See [Objectivism asks whether there is a moral fact; absolutism whether a rule is never broken](#/libs7102-l3/objectivism-absolutism-and-being-objective).
circumstantialism: *A resistance to absolutism (context/circumstances matter)*, not to be confused *with relativism (cultural context is all that matters)*; the engineer who uses different bridge designs *is rejecting absolutism, but they are not a relativist about physics* (slide 33). See [Objectivism asks whether there is a moral fact; absolutism whether a rule is never broken](#/libs7102-l3/objectivism-absolutism-and-being-objective).
blind loyalty: Loyalty *at all costs*, which *turns out to be a form of relativism (blind loyalty to gang/Mafia family/company/co-workers)*; loyalty itself is not intrinsically wrong (slides 31–32). See [Objectivism asks whether there is a moral fact; absolutism whether a rule is never broken](#/libs7102-l3/objectivism-absolutism-and-being-objective).
core values (tolerance): The values *where tolerance seems inappropriate (e.g. sexual harassment, fraud, corruption, murder)*; *only outside this core tolerance is meaningful* (slide 35). See [An objectivist can be tolerant; a relativist cannot defend tolerance](#/libs7102-l3/tolerance-without-relativism).
